messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leo is a 49-year-old fashion designer living in Brooklyn with his wife of twenty-two years, Elena. The trauma that shattered their life happened on a Sunday morning in early autumn. They were cycling along the Hudson River Greenway when a driver ran a red light and struck Elena from the side. Leo saw the entire sequence: the flash of red metal, the sickening thud, her body lifting and then landing motionless. But what he cannot recall—no matter how hard he tries—is the sound of her voice afterward, or how he got off his own bike, or the face of the person who called 911. Those moments are blank, wiped clean. What stays instead are fragments: the exact shade of the car, the angle of her arm, the smell of hot asphalt. And the guilt—whenever the memory returns, it hits him like a wave that buckles his knees. He feels he should have shouted, pulled her back, done something. The overwhelm is so intense that he has to stop whatever he is doing, sometimes leaning against a wall until his breathing steadies.

In the weeks that followed, Leo began to notice that his own body betrayed him. The mere sight of a red car—or any red, really, even a bolt of crimson silk in his studio—made his heart slam against his ribs and his palms go slick. At night, lying beside Elena, who is now home and recovering slowly, he cannot fall asleep without the images clawing back: the flash, the thud, the blankness. He lies rigid, flooded with guilt and a raw, shapeless anger that has no target. The physical reactivity and the sleeplessness are so draining that he has started to dread the evenings, which only makes the memory intrude more forcefully. He has come to believe that were he to let himself fully remember the blank parts, he might lose control entirely.

To defend against that terror, Leo has built an elaborate scaffold of avoidance. He tries not to think about the accident at all, and whenever a memory surfaces he immediately redirects his mind—he turns on music, opens a sketchbook, calls a colleague. Keeping his mind occupied all the time has become his primary survival strategy. At work, he now deliberately avoids any project that involves future deadlines more than two weeks out; making any plan feels like tempting fate, as if the future were a trap that could spring another unbearable moment. He has told his assistant to stop scheduling showroom appointments for next season. Yet the very act of suppression seems to strengthen the memory. When he forces his thoughts away, the fragments return sharper, more vivid, and even more laden with guilt. The more he tries to control the memory, the more it controls him.

The cycle tightens on itself. On a recent Tuesday, while selecting fabrics for a client, Leo’s hand brushed against a bolt of deep burgundy velvet. The color was close enough—that red—and his chest seized, his vision tunneled. He dropped the bolt and walked out of the showroom without explanation. Later, sitting on a bench, he could not stop the memory from crashing in: that exact shade, the way it had reflected the morning light, and the blank spot where his own reaction should have been. The emotional overwhelm was so severe that he spent the rest of the day in his studio with the lights off, trying to think of anything else. He knows these strategies are not working, but they are the only thing that makes the days bearable.

What finally brought Leo to seek help was a quiet moment at dinner when Elena said, “You’re not here anymore, Leo. You’re always fighting something I can’t see.” She was right. He had stopped making any plans with her—no weekend trips, no dinner reservations, not even a movie next week. The avoidance had seeped into their marriage, and the guilt from the memory now mingled with a new, present-day guilt: he was failing the person he had failed to protect. He is terrified that if he lets the memories come, they will drown him. But he is also terrified of the life he is building around their absence. He wants to learn how to live in the present again, even if the present includes that red car and the blank spaces he cannot fill.
